newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn wants to improve Bosnian refugees' treatment.
newsitem.headline: Bonn wants to improve Bosnian refugees' treatment.

text.p: Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, responding to tough criticism of Germany's repatriation of Bosnian refugees, said on Saturday he would visit the Balkan country to discuss the policy.
Kinkel said he would go to Bosnia with European Union commissioner Hans van den Broek soon to try to improve the way refugees were dealt with when they returned home.
"Let's not forget we are talking about people, some of whom have lived with us for many years. We can't just send them back overnight by a mechanical process," he said in a statement.
The only way to ensure the return of the refugees went smoothly was to have comprehensive information of every refugee's ethnic group, home town and religion, he said.
This could only take place in Germany, he said, adding he had discussed this with Interior Minister Manfred Kanther and representatives from Germany's regional states.
Kinkel's predecessor, Hans-Dietrich Genscher, and other public figures appealed on Friday for changes in the practice of forcibly repatriating Bosnian refugees.
They said the current policy could lead to increased tensions in Bosnia and was damaging Germany's international image.
They singled out the deportation this week of a group of Bosnian refugees from Berlin and Bavaria for criticism.
"Among those deported were pregnant women, patients receiving treatment for heart illness and other people whose deportation is incomprehensibe," they said.
They also said Germany was deporting people back to the Bosnian Serb entity, Republika Srpska, which they described as being "controlled by radical forces."
Even refugees from Srebrenica, a Moslem enclave overrun in 1995 by Serbs who expelled some 40,000 people and where 8,000 men remain unaccounted for, were being sent home, they said.
The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR has also criticised the criteria for deciding which refugees should go home first.
German officials have decided to send back single people and those without children first but the UNHCR has said a refugee's home region should be the most important factor.
Germany took in more than 300,000 Bosnian refugees, more than the rest of the European Union put together.
